newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Courtaulds shrugs off pound, viscose.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Courtaulds shrugs off pound, viscose.

text.p: International chemicals group Courtaulds Plc announced a modest rise in full-year pre-tax profits on Wednesday, shrugging off the depredations of a strong pound and continued problems with its oldest product, viscose.

Pre-tax profit rose by two percent to 134 million pounds ($221.7 million), towards the top end of analysts' forecasts, with the dividend rising by three percent to 16.4 pence. Sales slipped back seven percent to 2.1 billion pounds, partly reflecting the sale of some businesses last year.
The results gave a fillip to Courtaulds' sickly share price, which has retreated steadily this year as analysts focused on weak demand and oversupply of viscose.
Courtaulds shares rose 24 pence to 330-1/2 in early afternoon trading after touching a five-year low on Tuesday, but remained well below the 12 month peak of 490 pence touched in October last year.
Traders said there was optimism that the company and the stock had put the worst behind them.
Courtaulds, which has 85 percent of its sales overseas, said the strong pound, depressed viscose and rayon markets and the sale of non-core operations restrained the group's profit recovery.

But chief executive Gordon Campbell said the group was now in good shape as it strove to boost the proportion of sales and profits derived from the expanding areas of coatings and sealants, plastic polymers and new super-fibre Tencel.

"We have a problem with viscose, which is 10 percent of sales, we have some worries about the value of sterling, but apart from that I think most of our businesses are in very good shape," Campbell told Reuters.

Campbell, who took charge last July, said viscose would continue to account for a dwindling proportion of sales. Courtaulds is Europe's biggest and oldest producer of viscose, which has been hit by overcapacity and a switch by fashion designers away from printed cloth.

But the group's newest fibre Tencel, which is derived from woodpulp, provided cause for optimism, moving into what Courtaulds expects to be sustained profit for the first time, despite the heavy costs of building special production plants in Grimsby, England, and Alabama.
Tencel helped boost operating profits at fibres by 14 percent to 65 million pounds despite viscose, an improvement that was repeated at the other core businesses.

At Coatings and Sealants, which are centred on the aerospace, marine and construction markets as well as powder coatings for consumer goods, profits climbed by 13 percent to 81 million pounds despite sluggish European markets, with North America and the Far East seeing strong growth.

Profits also rose at the smaller Polymer Products division, which Courtaulds is keen to expand. The business makes specialist films and packaging for consumer goods and toiletries. Profit rose 22 percent to 22 million pounds despite disruption caused by transfer of production between two U.S. plants.
